opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nadia, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I work in a big warehouse, picking orders. The robots bring the shelves to me and I pick from them. I have to collect my daughter at five, so I hope that's all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, whatever. The AI doesn't pick the boxes, I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my problem isn't AI. It's the quota. The system counts every item I pick per hour, and if I'm slow I get a warning. That would carry on anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same. Hit my rate, do my shifts, try to get the day shift so I can be home for my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired. Not scared, just tired.

S0.say: Fine, whatever. The AI doesn't pick the boxes, I do.
S0.think: My problem isn't AI, it's the pick-rate quota. That carries on whatever happens.
S0.do: Hits her rate, works her shifts and tries to get days so she's home for her daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who'll suffer, if nobody hires beginners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I already have robots next to me. Slow AI on the computers doesn't change much. Maybe the system that sets our quotas gets smarter and pushes us harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down. Maybe ask about the training for the robot technician job they advertise sometimes, but it's hard with a child and shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Same as always, a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the technician training. Would you actually go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they paid for it and it was in work hours, yes. If it's evenings, no. Who would watch my daughter?

S1.say: It's the young ones who'll suffer if nobody hires beginners.
S1.think: I already work beside robots. Smarter software might just push the quotas harder.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and would go for robot technician training only if paid and in work hours.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a little more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say now office people know how it feels to be watched by a computer all day. Welcome to my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not my job they're cutting. But I don't trust the politicians to do anything useful for people like me, whatever they argue about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Work, pick up my daughter, sleep. Maybe put a little aside if I can, which I usually can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's someone else's storm this time.

S2.say: Now office people know how it feels to be watched by a computer all day.
S2.think: It's not my job being cut, and I don't trust politicians to do anything useful for people like me.
S2.do: Carries on working and tries to put a little aside, though she usually can't.
S2.feel: Uneasy, but it's someone else's storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should go to workers, not just the people who own shares. We never see any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is physical, so it stays in this one. But if house prices go up, my rent goes up, and my pay doesn't. And more people will come to the warehouse looking for work, so the managers can push the quota even harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for every overtime shift, look for a cheaper flat further out, and ask family if they can help more with my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm working harder just to stand still.

S3.say: The gains should go to workers, not just the people who own shares.
S3.think: My job stays, but rent rises, pay doesn't, and more jobseekers means harder quotas.
S3.do: Takes every overtime shift, looks for a cheaper flat further out and asks family to help more with childcare.
S3.feel: Working harder just to stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I saw this coming years ago. Nobody listened when it was only warehouse workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one where they don't need me anymore. The robots already bring the shelves. If a robot can also pick, I'm gone, and every warehouse round here goes the same way at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for benefits and any free training, even if it's evenings, and ask family to help more with my daughter. I'd look at cleaning jobs, shop jobs, anything, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not surprised, but very afraid for my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only train in work hours before. Now you'd do evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Before, I had a job. Here I don't. Everything changes when there's no job.

S4.say: I saw this coming years ago. Nobody listened when it was only warehouse workers.
S4.think: If a robot can pick too, I'm gone, and every warehouse round here goes the same way at once.
S4.do: Signs up for benefits and any free training, even evenings, asks family for more help and applies for cleaning or shop jobs early.
S4.feel: Not surprised, but very afraid for her daughter.
